LOL No, it's nothing to do with lens flair. It's pretty basic physics and camera design. See, the photons are reflecting off the surface of the vehicle. This will cause other photons to be diffuse and scatter. If you'd like to see an example, stand on a stage with the spotlights turned on - and have someone in the rear of the hall light a candle. Those photons are still moving at you at the speed of light, but they're being diffused by the photons that are hitting your retinas.

So, unless it's a whole lot of photons reaching you, you're not going to see them. They're not going to be picked up by the camera lens.

If they wanted to get pictures that included the stars, they'd want to do long exposures from a stable platform. This is a video camera, not a low-light lens attached to a stable platform.

You can recreate this for yourself - at your local high school theater department. There's just too many other photons being reflected from nearby surfaces and the exposures are much too rapid. It's pretty simple physics, methinks. Your human eye won't detect it, but if you shine one beam of light perpendicular to another beam of light, it will lessen the amount of light that makes it past that point.

For example, the Hubble Space Telescope takes exposures that last for several weeks in duration. That thing is probably doing 60 FPS. Less concentrated streams of particles are just not gonna hit the sensor. Lens flair is probably only tangentially related and wouldn't much matter in this case.
